title: Why Your Tendon Pain Is Not Healing (And the Slow Fix)
description:
Your tendon hurts for months because it heals slowly — it has far less blood flow than muscle, and rest alone never teaches it to handle load again. In this video: a two-part pain test, the science of slow tendon healing, and a gentle follow-along circuit of slow eccentrics. Educational content, not medical advice. If pain persists, see a licensed clinician.

#tendon #tendonpain #rehab #calisthenics #fitness #strength #achilles #isometrics

scenes.caption: DO THIS NOW
scenes.narration: Stop. Before I explain anything, do this test with me, right now. Take two fingers and press gently along the back of your ankle, right where the Achilles tendon runs down to your heel. Move slowly, from the calf down to the bone. Find the sorest spot. Now rate it, honestly, from zero to ten. Zero is nothing. Ten is the worst pain you can imagine. Got your number? Remember it, because that number is the whole point of this video, and we are going to test it again at the end. If pressing hurts, that is information, not a verdict. It tells you exactly where your tendon is struggling, and why everything you have tried so far has failed to fix it. Write the number down somewhere, on your phone, on a piece of paper, anywhere you will find it again. A real number, written down, is the only honest way to know whether the slow work ahead is actually doing its job.

scenes.caption: RATE YOUR PAIN 0-10
scenes.narration: Now the second test. Stand on one leg, rise up slowly onto the ball of your foot, and lower yourself back down even slower, taking a full five seconds to come down. That slow lowering is the movement this whole video is about. Rate the pain again, zero to ten. Was it worse than the press, or better? If the slow lowering hurts, your tendon is telling you it cannot handle load the way it should. Most people panic here and rest it completely. That is the first mistake, and it is exactly why your pain keeps coming back, month after month, no matter how many times you rest it. Pay attention to what the lowering reveals. Does the pain arrive at the very bottom, or halfway down? Does it fade once you are standing still again? Those details matter, because a tendon that hurts during the lowering but settles quickly is a tendon that can still be trained gently, while pain that lingers for hours afterwards means you need to back off and start even lighter.

scenes.label: WHY TENDONS HEAL SO SLOWLY
scenes.sub: tendon tissue has far less blood flow than muscle - so it repairs slowly
scenes.narration: Here is the science in two words: low flow. Your muscles are full of blood vessels, which is why a pulled muscle heals in weeks. Your tendons are almost the opposite. They have very little blood supply, and blood is what carries the building materials that repair tissue. So when a tendon gets damaged, the repair crew arrives late and works slowly. This is not your fault, and it is not because you are doing something wrong. It is the anatomy of the tissue itself, and once you understand that, everything about tendon pain starts to make sense. That is also why the usual fixes do not work. Ice numbs it for an hour. Rest feels good for a week, then the pain returns the moment you load it again, because nothing about the tendon itself has changed. The only honest way forward is to work with the slow biology, not against it, and to load the tendon at a pace it can actually adapt to.

scenes.head: STUDY - SLOW ECCENTRIC REHAB
lines: Slow eccentrics are the classic rehab protocol
for painful tendons: lower slowly under load.
Stay in a pain-free range, and progress
gradually, week by week, not day by day.
scenes.foot: Educational content, not medical advice - see a clinician for pain
scenes.narration: So what actually works? The classic rehab approach for painful tendons is slow eccentric loading. Eccentric just means the lowering phase, the part where the muscle lengthens under load. Instead of bouncing or jumping, you lower slowly and under control, the way you did in the test. Research and clinical practice keep returning to the same idea: gentle, slow, repeated loading is what tells a tendon to remodel and get stronger. This is not medical advice, and if your pain is sharp or persistent, see a licensed clinician. But the principle is simple: load it slowly, or it never learns to handle load at all. The key detail is the range you work in. Pain-free does not mean effortless, it means the discomfort stays low and settles within a day, never sharp and never worse the next morning. You start with a light version, maybe both feet instead of one, or a shorter range, and you add a little more load each week. Small steps, repeated for months, are what rebuild a tendon. Big jumps are what re-injure it.

scenes.title: WHERE THE PAIN SITS
scenes.narration: Picture the chain again. Muscle is the engine, and it heals fast because it is rich in blood. Bone is the lever, solid and slow to change. And between them sits the tendon, the cable, the part that carries every bit of force from the engine to the lever. When the cable is damaged, the engine still works fine, which is why you can feel strong and still be in pain. The pain sits in the cable, not the muscle. That is why stretching the muscle never fixes it, and why massaging the calf never fixes it either. You have to load the cable itself, slowly, and give it time. Think about what that means for training. Every jump, every sprint, every heavy lift passes through that one cable. The engine can be the strongest in the world and it does not matter, because the cable decides how much force actually reaches the ground. The fix is never to ignore the cable. It is to train it, slowly, until it can carry the load again.
Move one. Slow calf lower. Rise on both feet, lower on one, five slow seconds down. Gentle, no pain. Go.
Move two. Gentle wall sit. Back flat, knees slightly bent, and hold still. Easy load, no bouncing. Go.
Move three. Easy dead hang. Straight arms, feet lightly touching the floor if you need them. Hang long and still. Go.

scenes.label: THE HONEST TIMELINE
scenes.sub: tendon healing is measured in months - slow, steady loading wins
scenes.narration: Now the honest part, the part nobody selling a quick fix will tell you. Twelve weeks. That is the real timeline for a tendon to genuinely remodel and calm down, with slow loading three times a week. Not twelve days. Not a magic stretch. Twelve weeks of boring, patient, gentle loading. Most people quit in week three because nothing has changed yet, and then they say nothing works. The people who get better are the ones who understood the tissue they were dealing with. Slow tissue needs slow work, but slow work builds the kind of strength that does not disappear. Here is what those twelve weeks actually look like. The first month is mostly about learning the movements and finding the right load, and you may feel almost nothing changing. Around week six, the morning stiffness starts to fade. By week nine or ten, the pain number you wrote down at the start begins to drop.

scenes.caption: RETEST IN 12 WEEKS
scenes.narration: So here is your homework. In twelve weeks, do the same two tests again, in the same spot, with the same slow lowering, and rate the pain again, zero to ten. And today, tell me your starting number in the comments. Just the number. Five, three, seven. That number is your before picture, and it is the only measurement that matters. Next video, we go deeper into the one exercise that builds tendon strength without moving at all: isometrics. This is Wire Strength. Train the cable, slowly, and the cable will carry you again. And do not wait twelve weeks to check in. Test yourself every two weeks, same spot, same slow lowering, same honest rating, and watch the trend, not the daily noise. If the number is not moving by week six, that is useful information too, and it is worth talking to a clinician about.
